events.title: MCDB Dissertation Defense Seminar> The Regulation and Interactome of an H4K20-Specific Demethylase in Dosage Compensation of C. elegans
events.summary: In species that use sex chromosomes to differentiate between its sexes, there is a difference in sex chromosome number and the number of gene copies which results in unequal gene dosage. In species that cannot tolerate this imbalance in gene dosage, the dosage compensation process is applied in which the gene expression levels between the two sexes are made equal. In mammals, female somatic cells (XX) have one X chromosome inactivated to equalize to the single X chromosome in male somatic cells (XY). In C. elegans, hermaphrodites (XX) downregulate both X chromosomes by half to equalize to the single X chromosome in their male counterparts (XO). Dosage compensation in C. elegans is conducted primarily by the Dosage Compensation Complex (DCC), a multimeric set of proteins including a CondensinIDC complex and several additional proteins that bind, compact and downregulate the X chromosomes in hermaphrodites. One of the non-condensin proteins in the DCC is DPY-21, a Histone 4 Lysine 20 (H4K20)- specific demethylase. DPY-21 binds to the hermaphroditic X chromosomes and converts H4K20 di-methylation (H4K20me2) into mono-methylation (H4K20me1). This results in the enrichment of the repressive H4K20me1 mark on the X and the transcriptional downregulation of the X chromosomes. Although DPY-21 is part of the DCC, it localizes to the X chromosomes at a later stage of embryogenesis and does not bind mitotic chromosomes, contrasting to the other DCC components. Additionally, DPY-21 has been shown to have a DCC-independent role in the germline where dosage compensation in unrequired. This drives the question of the regulation of DPY-21 and its interactors in addition to the DCC. The first part of my thesis is the characterization of DPY-21 regulation through phosphorylation. Using CRISPR/Cas9 site-directed mutagenesis, I generated a dpy-21 phosphomutant C.elegans strain by mutating the phosphosites of DPY-21 into Alanines to render them non-phosphorylatable. Through physiological assays, I found that the dpy-21 phosphomutant C. elegans strain has defects in embryogenesis and larval stages. In embryogenesis, the phosphomutations disrupts DPY-21’s localization to the X chromosomes and delays the enrichment of H4K20me1 to the X chromosomes. Through biochemical and imaging analysis, I demonstrate that the global levels of 4K20me1 is increased in the phosphomutant strain, suggesting that the mutant protein may be hyperactive. At the larval stages, the dpy-21 phosphomutant strain exhibits developmental delay and increased propensity to form dauers. These defects are resolved by adulthood which implies that DPY-21’s activity is most critical in the embryonic and larval stages. The second part of my work revealed novel interactors of DPY-21. I conducted an immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS ) on DPY-21 to establish its interacting partners and found the kinase SPK-1 to be a top interactor of DPY-21. In spk-1 mutants, there is delayed H4K20me1 enrichment on the X chromosomes in embryogenesis which ultimately results in disrupted H4K20me1 enrichment on the X chromosomes in adults. This shows that SPK-1 may regulate DPY-21 although this may be indirect. Taken together, my work has characterized a novel dpy-21 mutant for the field that leads to its hyperactivity in generating H4K20me1 globally as well as the novel interactor SPK-1 that may regulate DPY-21.

events.title: BME Special Guest Lecturer
events.summary: BME Special Guest Lecturer: Stephane Avril Multiscale Digital Twins IN CARDIOVASCULAR MEDICINE Abstract: Aortic aneurysms and dissections require personalized therapeutic strategies to reduce the risk of catastrophic complications. This lecture introduces a multiscale digital-twin framework combining fast surrogate biomechanical models, machine-learning–based inverse identification, and tissue mechanobiology. At the clinical scale, latent-space representations enable rapid patient-specific simulation to predict complications such as endoleaks. At the material scale, inverse methods and neural-network constitutive models reveal regional tissue properties and rupture indicators. At the biological scale, growth-and-remodeling models describe how proteolytic injury, hemodynamics, and cellular processes drive disease progression. By integrating these components, digital twins become powerful tools to support diagnosis, intervention planning, and future therapies for delaying vascular aging. Bio: Stéphane Avril is Professor of Biomechanics and Biomedical Engineering at Mines Saint-Étienne, France, and Director of the SAINBIOSE laboratory (INSERM U1059). He received his PhD in Mechanical and Civil Engineering from Mines Saint-Étienne in 2002. His research focuses on biomechanics and mechanobiology of soft tissues, with particular emphasis on cardiovascular applications. His work combines medical imaging, experimental characterization, computational modeling, and patient-specific digital twins. He has led major research programs funded by the ERC, ANR, BPI France, and Horizon Europe. He is the recipient of an ERC Advanced Grant (JuvenTwin) and previously held an ERC Consolidator Grant. He has been a Visiting Professor at Yale University and Guest Professor at TU Vienna and TU Graz. He has authored more than 230 peer-reviewed publications and supervised over 50 PhD students and 25 postdoctoral researchers. He is cofounder of PrediSurge and KaomX, translating biomechanical research into innovative medical and research technologies. He was elected to the World Council of Biomechanics in 2026 and has received several international awards for his contributions to biomechanics. Websites: https://emse.fr/~avril https://sainbiose-lab.fr/

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. events.title: Housing First or Treatment First? Evidence from the VA's Homelessness Programs
events.summary: Debates in homelessness policy often pit Housing First programs, in which subsidized housing is offered unconditionally and immediately, against Treatment First interventions, which combine short-term housing with treatment for issues like substance use. I study a national sample of nearly 300,000 unhoused, mentally ill Veterans who are potentially eligible for the VA's Housing First program (known as HUD-VASH or VA Supportive Housing) or for a Treatment First program (offered by a variety of local contractors). Using an instrumental variables design, I find that enrolling in Housing First reduces three-year mortality by 4.6 percentage points relative to a no-program counterfactual. In contrast, Treatment First has no long-term effects on health. Housing First is also cost-saving, as it causes individuals to substitute away from lengthy inpatient stays.

events.title: MCDB Seminar Series> Identification of enhancer regulatory variants that shape root system architecture
events.summary: Variation in regulatory DNA is thought to be a major factor driving phenotypic variation in wild species as well as domestication of cultivated plants. Enhancers, a type of regulatory DNA sequence, regulate target gene expression in a spatiotemporal manner and can be relatively distal to their target genes, thus making them difficult to characterize. We performed a genome-wide association study and identified genetic variants associated with aspects of root system architecture in a collection of domesticated and wild tomato accessions. Using a massively parallel reporter assay, we tested and confirmed their relative allelic activity in vivo. A gene, PERI, associated with one of these variants is precisely spatiotemporally expressed in lateral root precursor cells. PERI expression varies according to its allele variant in cultivars within the association mapping panel and is required for lateral root development. Collectively, these data demonstrate the importance of enhancers in shaping root system architecture in tomato and its wild relatives. Bio: Siobhan specializes in the regulation of gene expression in plant roots. Her research integrates genomics, molecular biology, and bioinformatics to understand how transcriptional networks control root development and response to environmental stress. By dissecting these complex regulatory pathways, she aims to uncover the mechanisms that enable plants to adapt to changing conditions, contributing to advancements in agricultural biotechnology and crop improvement. Her work is pivotal in developing resilient plant varieties for sustainable agriculture.

events.summary: Ticket prices on our website reflect all-in pricing for purchases made online or by phone. This means the price you see includes the ticket price plus MUTO’s ticket processing fee. Tickets may be purchased with no included fees in person at The Ark during box office hours. Have Your Merry Christmas With Me This holiday season, acclaimed vocalist Kat Edmonson returns with a dazzling new chapter in her celebrated career: the November 6, 2026 release of her latest album, Have Your Merry Christmas With Me, followed by a nationwide tour beginning Thanksgiving and continuing through the end of December. Have Your Merry Christmas With Me by Kat Edmonson plays like the soundtrack to a classic romantic comedy—lush, witty, soulful, and filled with longing, flirtation, and holiday warmth. Romantic bossa novas mingle with a tropical, 1960s-cocktail-party take on “Jingle Bells,” the swinging jazz-gospel exuberance of “Hark! The Herald Angels Swing,” and an achingly soulful transformation of Allen Toussaint’s “It’s Raining” into “It’s Snowing.” Two beautifully crafted originals, “Have Your Merry Christmas With Me” and “Hush! There’s a Falling Snow,” feel instantly at home among the standards, with the timelessness of future holiday classics. Bringing the music to the stage, Kat Edmonson’s 2026 Have Your Merry Christmas With Me Holiday Tour promises an unforgettable evening of festive charm, featuring sparkling new selections alongside beloved songs from her acclaimed catalog. After enchanting audiences year after year, she returns with the warmth, wit, and effortless elegance that have made her one of today’s most distinctive jazz vocalists. Kat is a Songwriters Hall of Fame award-winning singer and songwriter whom The New York Times has described as having “an equal foothold in jazz, cabaret and vintage cosmopolitanism pop.” She has appeared on Austin City Limits, NPR’s Tiny Desk Concerts, A Prairie Home Companion, and The Tonight Show, and has performed at venues and festivals including Carnegie Hall, the Montreux Jazz Festival, and the Blue Note in Japan. Her original songs have appeared in film, television, and advertising. Edmonson also appeared as a 1930s jazz singer in Woody Allen’s Café Society and made her theatrical debut in the Drama Desk Award-nominated off-Broadway production The Hang by Taylor Mac and Matt Ray. As NPR observed, “Hearing Edmonson makes it virtually impossible to do anything but stop and listen.” Blending nostalgia, celebration, and holiday spirit, this concert feels both classic and new, with all the makings of a cherished seasonal tradition.

events.title: CCPS Photo Exhibition. This is the Place
events.summary: There are nearly one million refugees currently living in Poland. While the vast majority arrived from Ukraine, Poland has also welcomed forcibly displaced people from Central Asia, Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East. While refugees may be different, they all search for a place that reminds them of home. In *This Is The Place*, a project supported by the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR), Anna Liminowicz asked refugees to show what, in Poland, reminds them of their home. These portraits and the personalized confessions her subjects handwrote in their native languages tell poignant stories about safety and hope. Anna Liminowicz is an award-winning photographer and reportage journalist based in Warsaw, Poland. A frequent contributor to the *The New York Times*, *The Guardian*, *The Wall Street Journal*, *The Washington Post*, *El Pais*, *Der Spiegel* and UNHCR, Liminowicz divides her time between assignments and long-term personal projects, mainly focusing on social issues like identity and loss, and what uplifts her subjects. She has covered the war in Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, and received the 2022 Grand Press Photo Award for her project “Too Precious to Leave Behind”. events.title: From Printed Page to Research Data: Building Humanities Tools with AI Agents
events.summary: Attend a live demonstration, where Kwok-leong Tang, Harvard University, shows how AI coding agents, such as Claude Code, let a humanist build research tools by describing them in plain language, without being a trained programmer. Attend in person or register to join via Zoom (https://myumi.ch/Ax23x). No laptop or setup is needed for in-person attendees. The main demonstration is a full pipeline that turns printed materials into structured data: scanned pages go through OCR (turning page images into text), and the text then becomes a table of people, places, and dates, each checked against reference databases such as Wikidata and CBDB (China Biographical Database Project). Dr. Tang will also show other tools he has built this way, including a batch OCR tool, a converter for historical Chinese, Japanese, and Korean dates, a tool that suggests Library of Congress subject headings, and classroom history games made from primary sources. Throughout, we will look at how to check the agent's work and where this approach breaks down. Following the demonstration, 3:45-5:00 pm, Dr. Tang will host an optional office hour for in-person participants who are interested in discussing their own projects related to AI and East Asian studies. This informal session offers an opportunity to receive feedback, explore possible approaches, and consider both the potential and limitations of AI tools for your projects. Kwok-leong Tang serves as the managing director of the Digital China Initiative and a lecturer for the Department of East Asian Languages and Civilizations at Harvard University. By training, he is a historian. He received his bachelor’s and master’s degrees in history from the Chinese University of Hong Kong and a Ph.D. in history and Asian Studies from Pennsylvania State University. In recent years, he has focused on exploring the potential of new technologies in humanities research. He has organized and instructed workshops on adopting GenAI in Chinese studies and humanities research at Harvard and other institutions. The Deep Dive into Digital and Data Methods for Chinese Studies series is sponsored by the U-M Library (Asia Library) and the Lieberthal-Rogel Center for Chinese Studies. For inquiries, please contact asialibrary@umich.edu.
events.imageAlt: From Printed Page to Research Data: Building Humanities Tools with AI Agents

events.title: The Allocative Cost of War: A View to a Kill. . .ing of Productivity
events.summary: Why is war so economically costly? Our answer is that modern war lowers output not only by destroying productive factors, but also by making the surviving economy work less efficiently. Using uniquely comprehensive firm-level data collected during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, we document a dramatic collapse in allocative productivity in Ukraine. To sharpen identification and explore key mechanisms (including the role of war intensity, internal displacement, reallocation, and macroeconomic instability), we exploit spatial heterogeneity across Ukrainian districts and comparisons with Russian aggression in 2014 and the 2008 Global Financial Crisis. Our key policy implication is that restoring allocative efficiency–and preparing institutional arrangements that facilitate rapid reallocation in times of stress–is critical for sustaining economic capacity, defense, and national security.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: CSAS Lecture Series | Annihilation of Caste: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the Making of a Radical Dalit Humanism
events.summary: Please note: This lecture will be held in person and virtually on Zoom. If you would like to attend via Zoom, registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/Mpp5R This talk focuses on the intellectual and formidable anti-caste leader Dr. B. R. Ambedkar’s (1891–1956) multi-pronged – social, cultural and political – strategies of creating manuski (human dignity), dharmantar (religious conversion) and respectable samaj (community) in a doubly colonial – British and brahmanical context. To Ambedkar, the larger Indian society denied manuski to Dalits. The caste mechanism restricted Dalits claims to personhood as Dalit humanity itself was constituted as a state of injury and punishment. The consequences were particularly dangerous for Dalit women lacking even minimal security. As a result, Ambedkar and his associates focused on both—external and internal—changes to cultivate manuski. Ambedkar constituted a new Dalit woman through these inner resources and interrelated ideas of an intrinsically caring and civilized humanity. He along with his associates robustly worked on a multi-pronged strategy—social, educational, political, legal, and religious, to regenerate Dalits and not merely reform them like in the case of elite touchable reformers. Shailaja Paik is Charles Phelps Taft Distinguished Professor of History and affiliate faculty in women’s, Gender, and sexuality studies, sociology, and Asian studies at the University of Cincinnati. She is a 2024 MacArthur Foundation “genius” Fellow. Paik is also the founding executive director of the Institute for Just Futures. Her work analyzes the politics of caste, gender, class, and sexuality, by focusing on the ideas, actions, and lives of Dalits (“Untouchables”). She is the author of the prestigious awards-winning book *The Vulgarity of Caste: Dalits, Sexuality, and Humanity* (Stanford University Press, 2022) and *Dalit Women's Education in Modern India: Double Discrimination* (Routledge, 2014). Paik is co-editing the *Cambridge Companion to Dr. B.R. Ambedkar* (forthcoming) and *Caste, Race, and Indigeneity in South Asia and Beyond* (Forthcoming Routledge). Her research is funded by the MacArthur Foundation, the American Council of Learned Societies, the Stanford Humanities Center, the National Endowment for the Humanities, the American Institute of Indian Studies, Yale University, Emory University, the Ford Foundation, and the Charles Phelps Taft Research Center, among others. Paik has published several articles on a variety of themes, including kissing and nationalism, the politics of naming, Dalit and African American women’s solidarity, Dalit women’s education, and new Dalit womanhood in colonial India. Her scholarship and research interests are concerned with contributing to and furthering the dialogue in anti-race, anti-caste, and anti-patriarchy, human rights, anti-colonial struggles, transnational women’s history, and women-of-color feminisms. events.title: SRC Seminar Series Presents: Adolescence Post-Dobbs: The Changing Experience of Youth in America
events.summary: Join Zoom Meeting https://umich.zoom.us/j/96614746841?pwd=NsaP62jYD2RG9iznBdq7saPbixRP8P.1&jst=2 Meeting ID: 966 1474 6841 Passcode: 920742 Abstract Adolescence is a time of identity formation, when young people figure out who they are and who they want to be. One of the ways they do this is by considering the world around them, paying attention to social issues and starting to understand their society and their place in it. Laws and policies signal to young people what society thinks of their value, their role in society and their opportunities for the future. But the experience of growing up in the post-Roe v. Wade era looks very different from that before the 50-year precedent was overturned in 2022. Following the Dobbs v. Jackson Supreme Court decision, two-thirds of U.S. adolescents now live in a state with severely restricted or no legal abortion access. As a result, today’s young people are coming of age in what has been termed an “era of rights retractions.” This talk will provide a data-based account of how, following Dobbs, the experience of adolescence and young adulthood in America has fundamentally changed and how rights retractions are not only affecting those who need an abortion – they are shaping an entire generation. Biography: Dr. Julie Maslowsky is Associate Professor of Health Behavior and Clinical Sciences at the University of Michigan School of Nursing, Associate Professor of Health Behavior and Health Equity at the University of Michigan School of Public Health, and Research Associate Professor at the UM Institute for Social Research. She is a developmental psychologist and population health scientist who studies adolescent health, with a focus on sexual and reproductive health including contraception and abortion. Her research integrates adolescent developmental science with population and reproductive health to inform developmentally appropriate policies and practices on adolescent sexual and reproductive health.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Probability and Analysis: Strongly log-concave measures and lattices
events.summary: Let L be a lattice in R^n. Suppose that L has the property that the determinant of every non-zero sublattice L' of L is larger than one. We prove that there exists a symmetric random vector X on R^n with a smooth, strictly positive density f on R^n simultaneously enjoying the following two properties: a) f is strongly log-concave; b) X + L is uniform on R^n/L. Moreover, the existence of such a density f on R^n characterizes this determinant condition imposed on L. This construction connects several problems in lattice theory to established results in convex geometry. We discuss a range of applications. This is joint work with Victor Reis and Thomas Rothvoss.

events.summary:
Make a Reservation 
There will be two separate seatings at 7:30pm & 9:30pm for this performance. Doors open at 5pm for dinner. Seating begins at 6pm for “Dinner & a Show”. The second show starts seating at 9pm.
With Detroit’s own Louis Jones on the drums and Noah Jackson on bass. 
A native of Camden, New Jersey, Eric Lewis began his musical studies at 2 years old and would ultimately receive the Rodger’s and Hammerstein full merit scholarship to the Manhattan School of Music. A Dean’s List student, upon graduation, he toured the world, recorded and performed with Wynton Marsalis & the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra, Elvin Jones, Cassandra Wilson, Roy Hargrove, and John Hendricks among others. In 1999, Eric won the Thelonious Monk International Piano Competition, at the time, the most coveted prize in all of Jazz. A decade into his career, he reemerged as ELEW and began fusing his piano techniques with rock guitar-based ideas and experimental prepared piano methods, generating a powerful crossover brand he coined “Rockjazz”. Over the course of multiple award winning, critically acclaimed albums, ELEW has re-imagined songs by The Killers, Nirvana, Coldplay and Michael Jackson to name a few. Throughout his career he has built an elite fanbase of some of the most distinguished leaders and celebrities such as Leonardo DiCaprio, Gerard Butler, Barack and Michele Obama, Prince Albert II, Will Smith, Eli Roth, Al Pacino and the list goes on… Inspired by the European masters of Baroque Counterpoint, ELEW has innovated the technique of simultaneously executing two independent melodies which precisely detail harmonic forms bursting with idiomatic verisimilitude and wide ranging historical references while flawlessly maintaining the idiosyncratic Afrocentric timing at the core of Jazz improvisation. 
He has named this technique Counterbop. His album Cubism – ELEW plays Rosenwinkel, a solo piano exploration of contemporary jazz legend Kurt Rosenwinkel provides perspective an insight into the nature of what Counterbop is and how it may be implemented. In addition to piano performance, appearing in and scoring for film, ELEW is a prominent international DJ. He has has created disco infernos for multiple events such as The World Economic Forum, TED, Art Basel, A-list Oscar parties, the Monte-Carlo Gala, the Cannes Film Festival and multiple celebrity birthdays and weddings. In some cases, ELEW places the turntables within the piano, seamlessly executing transitions and improvisations all while generating a pleasing frenzy on the dance floor. This has lead to him creating yet another brilliant innovation he calls Piano Turntablism . He literally plays two different yet recognizable songs simultaneously as a Dj would but on the Piano. All while maintaining the type of euphoric atmosphere one would experience at an over-the-top Las Vegas mega club or an epic music
festival. ELEW is a genuine master of the piano and artistic genius.

events.title: Past Matters: Environments and Methods in Medieval Europe and the Mediterranean
events.summary: The field of medieval environmental history has grown immensely from its inception 30 years ago. While scholars of the classical past and modern period registered environmental changes made by their powerful states a little earlier, the topic caught on more slowly in the medieval field, where small and ineffective states posed different methodological challenges. It took different ways of studying nature to see how environments changed in Europe and the Mediterranean during the millennium between 500 and 1500 CE. Scholars of the medieval environment of necessity adopted an acrobatic approach to the past, bringing together the usual tools of the historian -- close textual analysis – with archaeology, archaeobotany, and scientific studies of pollen distribution, weather patterns, and the contents of middens. Today, the field of medieval environmental history represents one of the most methodologically diverse and inventive among any branch of history. This one-day conference, with an opening session on the previous afternoon, will appraise the major developments and turning points of the last 30 years in medieval environmental history with papers from some of the leading scholars in the field. Since one of the pioneers in medieval environmental history, Paolo Squatriti, has been on the faculty of the U of M for 25 years, the conference will take cues from his seminal works and methodological turns. Panels will offer papers within the following themes: 1. History in the mundane 2. Historical agency and unexpected actors 3. The Mediterranean as a place of hybridity 4. Materiality and the past 5. Science in the service of history. Featuring: Jon Arnold (University of Tulsa) Henrik Dey (Hunter College) Hussein Fancy (Yale University) Benjamin Graham (University of Memphis) Richard Hoffman (York University) Alyssa Kotva (The Ohio State University) Jamie Kreiner (University of California, Los Angeles) Stephanie Leitzel (Cornell University)

events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: Bid Timing and Market Efficiency in the Energy Transition.
events.summary: Utility-scale batteries play an increasingly active role in electricity markets by arbitraging energy across time, yet their efficiency depends critically on market design. This paper studies a prevalent feature of real-time electricity auctions: bid lead time, which requires batteries to commit bids in advance of dispatch. Using comprehensive 15-minute bidding and settlement data for all utility-scale batteries in ERCOT from 2018–2025, we document active dynamic bidding, rapid responses to price shocks, and the importance of recent price information for forecasting. We develop an equilibrium model of electricity markets with dynamic battery bidding and show that longer bid lead times substantially reduce operational efficiency and profits, and dampen complementarity between batteries and renewable energy. Allowing bids to depend on state of charge significantly mitigates these losses. Our results highlight bid lead time as a key determinant of battery performance and market outcomes.

events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. events.summary: Fri | Oct 30 Sets at 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE(opens in new tab) About the Artist Internationally renowned bassist and Mack Avenue recording artist, Rodney Whitaker is one of the world’s renowned double bass performers, educators, mentors and is dedicated to inspiring and growing the next generation of jazz educators and musicians. A Detroit native, he grew up in the city soaking in the sounds of jazz and classical music and working with the finest musicians in the city. Building on his Detroit roots and enormous talent, Whitaker went on to earn an international reputation as one of the world’s finest jazz double bass performers. He completed a seven-year tenure as bassist with the Wynton Marsalis’ Sextet, the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra and has toured the world over the last twenty-six years, collaborating with over 100+ legendary performing jazz artists and leading symphony orchestras across the world. Featured on more than 100+ recordings – from film to compact discs – Whitaker’s film scores, China, directed by Jeff Wray, was released on PBS Fall 2002 and Malaria and Malawi, released on PBS Fall 2010. In 2011, he was nominated for an EMMY for the ‘Original Music’ category, “Malawi and Malaria: Fighting to Save the Children” produced by Robert Gould and Sue Carter. Whitaker collaborated with musicians Phil Dwyer and Alan Jones on “Let Me Tell You About My Day,” produced by Alma Records and was nominated for a Juno Award in 2006 for Traditional Jazz Album of the Year, Canada’s equivalent to the United State of America’s Grammy. He is a full professor of jazz double bass and director of jazz studies at Michigan State University where he has built one of the leading jazz degree granting programs offering both a bachelor’s and master’s degrees in Jazz Performance. events.title: Korean Performing Arts Initiative | Ensemble PHASE
events.summary: Ensemble PHASE is a collective of musicians dedicated to experimental music that brings traditional Korean instruments into dialogue with diverse musical languages. Since its founding in 2017, the ensemble has performed internationally, released three albums, and commissioned and premiered nearly 50 new works in collaboration with leading artists from Korea and around the world. For this special performance, Ensemble PHASE presents a program inspired by the life and legacy of Ilhan New, the Korean American entrepreneur, philanthropist, and University of Michigan alumnus. Through innovative musical interpretations, the performance explores the intersections of Korean and American experiences, offering a fresh artistic perspective on New’s remarkable life and enduring legacy. Program Overview This two-part program traces two defining periods in the life of Dr. Ilhan New: his early years in the United States after leaving Korea as a child, and his return to Korea, where he devoted himself to business, philanthropy, and the cause of Korean independence. Part I: Life in America — Traditional Korean Music Through a selection of traditional Korean music, the first half of the program reflects on New’s journey from his childhood in Korea to his experiences building a life in America. Each piece evokes a chapter of his personal story, from memories of his homeland and the voyage across the Pacific to the challenges of adapting to an unfamiliar culture, the perseverance required to pursue his education, and the beginning of a lifelong partnership with his wife. Part II: Return to Korea — Contemporary Compositions The second half explores New’s return to Korea and the lasting impact of his work through contemporary compositions by composers Edward Schocker, Dana Kaufman, and Hyoshin Na. These works reflect on his entrepreneurial vision, the tragedy of Korea’s division, and his commitment to the nation’s independence. The program concludes with *The Twenty Million* by Edward Schocker, a world premiere honoring New’s enduring legacy and his vision of dedicating his fortune to the advancement of future generations through education. Bringing traditional Korean music into dialogue with newly composed works, Ensemble PHASE offers an artistic portrait of a remarkable Korean American life shaped by migration, perseverance, service, and an enduring commitment to his homeland. *If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at outreachkorea@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.*

events.title: Department Colloquium | Horizon-Scale Modeling of Black Holes
events.summary: Recent developments have ushered in a new era in the field of black hole astrophysics, providing our first direct view of the remarkable environment near black hole event horizons. These observations have enabled astronomers to confirm long-standing ideas on the physics of gas flowing into black holes with temperatures that are hundreds of times greater than at the center of the Sun. In this talk I will describe the successes and challenges of theoretical models of black hole accretion on event horizon scales in the context of these observational advances. I will conclude with ideas on how the interplay of theory and observations can be used to measure the spin of black holes and test the long-standing prediction that the rotational energy of black holes can be extracted to power astrophysical jets.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show
events.summary: Jack Tucker is hilariously awful, and that’s precisely the point. The Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show is the misguided brainchild of Zach Zucker, a performer who is celebrated for blending virtuosic clowning with razor-sharp satire. His character Jack Tucker is a well-respected journeyman and bonafide legend on the Upstate New York regional comedy scene, a catastrophically overconfident stand-up comedian whose hacky punchlines, misplaced swagger, and desperate need to be adored convince him that he’s going to make it big any day now. As his jokes collapse and his bravado frays, the show exposes the fragile ego beneath the spotlight and the quiet terror behind the mic. Equal parts parody, performance art, and masterclass in comedic tension, Jack Tucker Comedy Standup Show walks a thrilling line, with Zach Zucker’s physical control and improvisational daring bringing both discipline and danger to the chaos. Zucker, whose clown lineage dates to the famous École Philippe Gaulier in France, the training ground for actors such as Sacha Baron Cohen, Helena Bonham Carter, Emma Thompson, and many others, is a cult favorite on the international comedy circuit, known for his always sold-out Stamptown Comedy and a forthcoming Netflix special. Recommended for mature audiences.

events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. events.title: Small Works: Prints & Book Objects from Detroit, 2020–2026
events.summary: Small Works Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026 October 27 - November 19 Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm. Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space. This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.
events.imageAlt: Small Works: Prints & Book Objects from Detroit, 2020–2026

events.title: Human Connection
events.summary: For a parking map and other helpful information, please visit the link on our website PLAN MY VISIT Take a journey from loneliness to human connection with this collection of LGBTQ dance performers/scholars from Ann Arbor, Michigan! We seek to define partnering, understand what it means in a traditional sense, and find ways to subvert the status quo -- while building meaningful connection between performers and communities. The movement concepts and ideas for “Human Connection” have been building for over 2 years within Dance Uprising’s body of work as well as in the bodies of the dancers themselves. The choreographic process for this work began in earnest in the spring of 2026. We utilize a movement form called Nontraditional Partnering, in which the roles of base and flyer are often interchangeable. Our choreographic process combines rigorous modern dance training with partnering and idiosyncratic movement development to create a totally unique piece. Research based dance choreography and performance is built upon informative articles, books, podcasts, and other media resources. These text and audio based selections inform our idiosyncratic movement development, relationship building between dancers on the stage, and the overall milieu in which the choreography takes place. In addition to the choreography itself, several production elements have gone into the development of this show. The sound score for this work features a piece written and performed by Detroit-based musician Max Popkin, as well as found sound. These are edited together to create a bespoke soundscape as the dancers perform onstage. Costume design for this work includes hand-painted costume pieces as well as thoughtfully curated items. We invite the Canton public – youth and adults alike – to join us for our debut Canton performance, supported by Village Arts Factory funding this year. Thank you for supporting the performing arts! “Human Connection” is a 1-hour performance, followed by a talk-back with the choreographer and dancers onstage. It is to be held at The Village Theatre in Canton, MI, on Thursday, November 12, 2026, at 6:00 p.m. There will be an accompanying movement workshop, open to the public, scheduled for earlier in the same week. Details will be announced.

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.
events.imageAlt: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”

events.title: Tiffany Gridiron
events.summary: Fri | Oct 23 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Tiffany Gridiron is a gifted jazz vocalist and songwriter who radiates joy and generosity on stage, even when singing the most haunting of songs. Her sultry vocals and playful approach have excited audiences in the United States, Japan, Finland and South Korea. Tiffany’s love of singing began as a child in her family church where both of her parents served as musicians. In her early twenties, inspired by the debut album of Jill Scott, Tiffany sought out voice lessons that serendipitously put her in contact with the amazing jazz vocalist and educator Sunny Wilkinson. Through jazz standards, Sunny introduced Tiffany to a world of poetry and improvisation that would profoundly impact the rest of her life. Studying works of Billie Holiday, Ella Fitzgerald, Sarah Vaughn and many other vocal legends helped Tiffany to find her own voice and style. Tiffany recorded five CDs of jazz standards, released by SONY RECORDS in Japan that have featured such greats as pianists Hank Jones, Tadataka Unno, drummer Omar Hakim, and many others. In 2019, Tiffany’s longtime friend and collaborator Kris Johnson approached her about producing a project where her gifts as a songwriter could be featured. The result was “From My Heart to Yours”, Tiffany’s most personal album to date. Released in September of 2023 on all digital platforms, five of the album’s eight songs feature lyrics penned by Tiffany Gridiron and co-composed by Kris Johnson. Kris also arranged, played trumpet and served as producer on the project, with Brendon Davis (piano), Jonathan Muir-Cotton (bass), Nate Winn (drums), and Vivienne Smith (background vocals) also adding their breathtaking artistry to this material. You can now catch Tiffany at venues in the Midwest and East coast, performing her originals, jazz standards, and other songs that explore the nuances of the human condition. Her deep appreciation for music as a tool for healing, inspires Tiffany to use her voice to nurture connections between people and hearts. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Austin Zhu, carillon
events.summary: Economics graduate student Austin Zhu performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: Gender: New Works, New Questions: Gestating Judaism with Cara Rock-Singer
events.summary: How do reproductive practices shape religious traditions, and how can the labor of reproduction become a site of feminist intervention? Join the Institute for Research on Women & Gender for the latest installment of Gender: New Works, New Questions, featuring Gestating Judaism: The Corporeal Technologies of American Jewish Religion by Cara Rock-Singer, assistant professor of Judaic Studies at the University of Michigan. In Gestating Judaism, Rock-Singer examines how reproductive practices shape the transmission and reinvention of American Judaism. Bringing together religious rituals, such as the mikveh, with contemporary practices like fertility treatments, she challenges conventional distinctions between religion, science, and politics. Through an innovative approach she calls “ethnodrashy,” Rock-Singer explores how Jewish feminists use reproductive labor to engage with questions of theology, identity, and political life. The event will feature a panel discussion with Rock-Singer, Liz Roberts, professor of anthropology, and Lisa Disch, professor of political science. The conversation will be moderated by IRWG director and professor of women’s and gender studies, Melynda Price. Drawing on perspectives from religious studies, anthropology, political science, and gender studies, the panel will explore how reproductive bodies become sites of religious meaning, feminist engagement, and cultural change.

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

Members of the Michigan Irish American Hall of Fame, Blackthorn offers shows that involve a musical ramble across Ireland. Traditional songs of emigration, ballads, shanties and jigs and reels combine with some of Ireland’s best contemporary songs for a musical experience that is uniquely Irish. Each of the band’s members plays multiple instruments, including flute, accordion, tin whistle, fiddle, banjo, cittern, bodhran, and more. events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.summary: Kathleen Beck performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media.
