events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Demetrius Nabors
events.summary: Sat | Oct 24 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Demetrius “Krayon” Nabors is a prominent pianist, composer, producer, and arranger, celebrated in both the Detroit area and the national contemporary jazz scene. His music reflects a rich tapestry of influences, including gospel, jazz, classical, and blues, all of which are evident in his compositions and performances. A two-time winner of the Detroit Music Award for Outstanding Gospel/Christian Musician, Demetrius holds both Bachelor’s and Master’s Degrees in Jazz Studies from the University of Michigan. His talents have taken him to stages in Europe and Africa, as well as to national television, including a memorable appearance on the former “Arsenio Hall” show. His exceptional skills have drawn the attention of numerous high-profile artists, including R&B singer KEM, flutist Althea Rene, guitarist Tim Bowman, and trumpeter Willie Bradley. Demetrius’s productions have achieved notable success on the Billboard charts, including two #1 hits for KEM’s singles “Nobody” and “It’s You” (2014), a #2 for Willie Bradley’s “It’s On Now” (2020), a #5 for Althea Rene’s “Barbara Mae” (2019), and a #1 for Tim Bowman’s “Fireball” (2021). Additionally, “Nobody” was nominated for Best Traditional R&B Performance at the 57th Grammy Awards. Demetrius’s discography features five critically acclaimed releases: “A Journey Within Part I” (2011), “Christmas with Krayon” (2012), “A Journey Within Part II” (2014), “Perseverance” (2021), and “Evolution EP” (2022). He thrives on the energy of live performance, a passion that shines through in his music and resonates deeply with his dedicated fan base. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: LRCCS Noon Lecture Series | Chinese and Muslim Refugees on the Tibetan Frontier, 1860–1965
events.summary: From 1860 onward, frequent wars and disasters claimed millions of lives in Northwest China. More than one million Chinese and Muslims sought refuge on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau. This talk explores the diverse experiences of these refugees as they crossed multiple ethnocultural and administrative boundaries, lived alongside Tibetans, and forged new homelands during China’s transition from empire to nation-state. Gyatso Marnyi is a historian of empires and frontiers in Asia. Combining textual sources with ethnographic fieldwork, his research examines interactions and exchanges between China and surrounding Asian regions from the fourteenth to the twentieth century. He is currently completing a monograph that explores the uneven experiences of Tibetan, Mongol, Chinese, and Muslim communities during China’s transition from empire to nation-state on the Inner Asian frontier. *Part of the International Institute Theme Year: Sovereignty* https://ii.umich.edu/ii/news-events/all-events/theme

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Marquis Hill
events.summary: Wed | Nov 4 Set 7pm $95 Dinner & Show $50 Cover Only RESERVE TABLE About the Artist One of the finest trumpeters in jazz today, Marquis Hill is also a composer and bandleader whose comprehensive vision highlights the unity and continuity within the musical heritage of AfricanAmericans. On acclaimed albums like his latest, Modern Flows Vol. II, and his 2016 breakout project, The Way We Play, Hill and his working band, the Blacktet, use their next-level musicianship and deeply interactive dynamic to break down the barriers separating bop, hip-hop, R&B and electronic music. Born in Chicago in 1987 and raised on the city’s South Side, Hill absorbed the jazz tradition both formally-he holds a bachelor’s in music education as well as a master’s in jazz pedagogy-and informally, gaining knowledge from his elders on gigs and at jam sessions. By the time he won the Thelonious Monk Institute of Jazz competition in the fall of 2014, his reputation for fluid virtuosity was firmly established in the Midwest-as a member of the Chicago Jazz Orchestra, an in-demand sideman and a leader with several buzz worthy self-released discs to his credit. Since that watershed victory, Hill has garnered glowing coverage in outlets like the New Yorker, the New York Times, JazzTimes, NPR Music and DownBeat, where he topped the “Rising Star- Trumpet” category in the 2016 Critics Poll. As he’s maintained a nonstop touring schedule with the Blacktet, he’s also supported and guested with a jazz who’s who that includes Marcus Miller, Dee Dee Bridgewater, Boney James, Kurt Elling, Joe Lovano and Hill’s trailblazing Chicago peer Makaya McCraven. events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Dave McMurray
events.summary: Sat | Oct 31 Sets 7pm & 9pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE(opens in new tab) About the Artist Dave McMurray’s move to Blue Note Records is a reunion of sorts, given the long history the saxophonist shares with the label’s president, and fellow Detroit native, Don Was. McMurray was a member of Was’ genre-defying unit Was (Not Was), first working together on the band’s self-titled 1981 debut. He’s played on all of the band’s albums and many other Was produced projects in the years since. When Was signed McMurray to Blue Note, the saxophonist says that he gave him no imperatives as to which artistic paths to take. “It was one of those situations in which he just said, ‘Do it,'” McMurray explains. McMurray has cemented his reputation for versatility by playing with a vast array of musicians that include B.B. King, The Rolling Stones, Bob Dylan, Iggy Pop, Patti Smith, Bonnie Raitt, Johnny Hallyday, Gladys Knight, Albert King, Nancy Wilson, KEM, Bootsy Collins, Herbie Hancock, Geri Allen, and Bob James. McMurray sounds as assured and inspired in a rock, R&B, funk, pop or folk setting as he does playing hard bop. McMurray attributes his saxophone sound and improvisational approach to growing up in Detroit. “Every time I hear an instrumentalist from Detroit play, it feels like they are singing. I don’t care if it’s Yusef Lateef, James Carter or Kenny Garrett. All of those saxophonists incorporated incredible technique too. But they had this singing quality in their playing. I think people hear that and connect with that aspect of it,” McMurray says. For sure, McMurray stands on Detroit’s mighty music legacy that includes the influential Motown sound, P-Funk, numerous rock acts such as Stooges and the MC5, electronica-music pioneers Carl Craig, Moodymann and Theo Parrish; and hip-hop icons – J Dilla, Eminem and Slum Village. And let’s not forget the legion of jazz artists from Detroit that include Elvin Jones, Betty Carter, Milt Jackson, Regina Carter and Geri Allen. McMurray’s journey into music began when he started playing clarinet as kid, and inspired by his older brother’s interest in the saxophone he decided he wanted to learn that instrument, too. He counts seeing Cannonball Adderley perform on The Steve Allen Show as a defining moment in his childhood. While in high school, McMurray attended Cranbook Academy of Arts’ noted summer program, Horizons Upward Bound. He eventually got a scholarship to attend the private school. McMurray furthered his education by attending Wayne State University, where he earned degrees in psychology and urban studies. While making his way on Detroit’s bustling music scene, McMurray played with the avant-garde jazz ensemble, Griot Galaxy, founded in 1972 by saxophonist Faruq Z. Bey. But McMurray’s catholic taste in music opened the doors for him to explore beyond the realms of jazz. “Any music that I heard – and continue to hear – I can see myself playing it,” McMurray asserts. “It could be rock, jazz, R&B, whatever.” And that’s a good explanation for his multifaceted career. RESERVE TABLE(opens in new tab)

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

events.title: Small Works: Prints & Book Objects from Detroit, 2020–2026
events.summary: Small Works Prints & Book Objects from Detroit 2020–2026 October 27 - November 19 Public Reception: Friday, November 13 from 4:30-6pm. Small Works was a print shop ran by Li Chen & Gerald Schulze, in Detroit, MI, from 2020–2026. Mariana Matos joined as the studio assistant, and later studio manager, in 2024. Over those six years, the business grew from an extension of their design practice to a community space that hosts more than 70 classes a year, open studio for the public, and year long funded fellowships that investigate practice in art and design related to the Book Arts. In 2026, they decided to expand community programming, and to accommodate this expansion closed Small Works, and formed Center for the Book Arts Detroit (BAD) which operates in the same space. This exhibition is a eulogy for the former Small Works shop, and a celebration of all the people who made work here. It also serves to show what is possible as a community, when they share space and create work together. The work featured is a collection of things printed by Small Works, by their studiomates Diskette Press, the publisher Maamoul Press, and by the community that uses the space.

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.

events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.summary: Sat | Nov 28 Shows 7pm & 9pm $125 Dinner & Show $75 Cover Only Reserve Table About the Artist With a voice that bridges generations, Stella Cole has cultivated over 2 million social media followers through her fresh interpretations of timeless songs by iconic artists, including Judy Garland, Frank Sinatra, and Nat “King” Cole. Often described as a Laufey-meets-Bublé sensation, Cole brings a fresh interpretation of classic repertoire to a new generation. While she was raised in rural Illinois on Hollywood musicals like Singin’ in the Rain and The Wizard of Oz, Cole told ELLE that she “never expected this life,” earning praise for her soulful interpretations of the Great American Songbook from legends including James Taylor, DavidFoster, and Michael Bublé. She’s performed on The TODAY Show, Live with Kelly and Mark, Tamron Hall, and stages thoroughout the U.S., Europe, and Asia. “It’s amazing to think that this music can be a balm for people’s stress and anxiety,” says Stella. “Don’t forget, these songs helped people get through the Great Depression and World War II. events.title: IES Energy Seminar Series - Don’t Blink! Seeing and defining high-temperature chemistry on the microsecond scale
events.summary: Abstract: Launching the next generation of satellites, producing high-fidelity nano-materials, and preventing fire spread all rely on complex phase change and rapid chemical reactions. However, the coupling of these processes as well as the fundamental reaction kinetics is poorly understood owing in large part to the difficulty in observing the highly reactive phenomena on relevant time and length scales. In this talk, I outline a multi-method approach for applying optical diagnostics and novel modelling techniques in complex operating environments to identify key drivers of reactivity, including multi-phase interactions and key gas-phase reaction mechanisms with a focus on the novel analytical methodologies developed. Key to many of these processes is the high-temperature gas-phase reactivity of base fuels or stable intermediates, with the potential for reaction mechanisms defining millisecond scale phenomena to encompass hundreds of possible reactions. I will highlight the role of highly repeatable shock tube experiments with high-fidelity diagnostics in unlocking the fast kinetics (<10 µs) behind these complex processes as well as how we utilize the laser induced shocking of solid materials to understand their thermal decomposition in extreme environments. In addition to highlighting the role of temperature on the gas-phase chemistry, I will also focus on the role of pressure in driving the multi-phase reactivity and phase change in propellant and energetic material applications. Biography: Dr. Rachel Schwind is a Lecturer in Experimental Thermofluids at the University of Edinburgh. Her expertise is in reaction kinetics and complex phase change with a focus on novel reactive materials and high-pressure heterogeneous chemistry with applications including green propulsion, materials synthesis, and energetic materials. Schwind's research focuses on merging fundamental chemical kinetics studies with complex application environments, including the development of novel analytical techniques and experimental design to provide improved understanding of key reactive drivers and kinetic pathways. Prior to joining the University of Edinburgh, Dr. Schwind was at Brown University, first as a postdoc and then as a Senior Research Associate overseeing the experimental activity in the Goldsmith Lab for Chemical Kinetics. She received her Masters and PhD in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Michigan, during which time she served as a visiting researcher at Argonne National Laboratory, first through a US Department of Energy SCGSR Fellowship and then as an NSF Intern. Her expertise in fast reaction kinetics of novel systems has been recognized with multiple invited seminars and panels, including selection for the Future of Combustion Research specialist panel by the Combustion Institute and a 40 under 40 e-Lecture on Combustion. For the most up to date information on the location, please check the related link the week of this event

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: AIM Seminar: Programmable Collective Dynamics in Active Matter and Robot Swarms
events.summary: Abstract: Collective systems are able to exhibit complex global dynamics through relatively simple local interactions, and they give us a powerful connection between nonequilibrium physics, active matter, and robotics. In this talk, I will present our work on understanding and controlling collective behavior across theoretical and experimental systems. I will first discuss experimental work involving magnetic microrobot collectives in which competing pairwise interactions enable reconfiguration between distinct states, locomotion, and environmental interactions. And when heterogeneity and asymmetric interactions are introduced, they can be used to program self-organization and generate various collective behaviors that include phase separation, morphology changes, and object manipulation. At the more theoretical level, I will discuss swarmalators, which are agents that simultaneously swarm and synchronize, and I will show how chirality, heterogeneity, multiple internal phases, and nonreciprocal interactions can enable fascinating and non-intuitive collective states, as well as be exploited to systematically control the collective to exhibit desired shape formation, navigation, and object manipulation, such that principles from active matter can be used for programmable collective robotic systems. Contact: Silas Alben

events.title: Citations Beyond “Playing the Game:” Building a Robust Citation Policy
events.summary: In this workshop, participants will bring a personal research project to assess or map out a citation policy that reflects their commitments and values. Sara Ahmed tells us that “citations can be feminist bricks: they are the materials through which, from which, we create our dwellings.” Our citation policies “affec[t] the kind of house” in which we spend our intellectual lives (Living a Feminist Life 15). In this workshop, participants begin by reflecting on their various commitments and values before engaging in a discussion of the shared reading. The session concludes with individual and collaborative workshop time targeting feasibility in their designs. Participants assess citations in a recent project to determine the extent to which they have used citations to build the kind of “dwelling” they want to occupy and explore options for further renovating. Alternatively, participants may bring a project they have not yet researched fully in order to map a citation policy for that project. Qualifiers: This is a workshop especially designed for those in the humanities, social and applied sciences. Before the workshop, we ask that you read an eight-page excerpt (sent to those who register) from Ahmed’s Living a Feminist Life. Presented by April Conway and Laura Clapper, Sweetland Center for Writing Faculty

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Joshua Radin
events.summary: Ticket prices on our website reflect all-in pricing for purchases made online or by phone. This means the price you see includes the ticket price plus MUTO’s ticket processing fee. Tickets may be purchased with no included fees in person at The Ark during box office hours. Joshua Radin emerged in 2004 as an empathetic, engaging, and often enthralling troubadour. Over the years, he’s tallied north of 1 billion streams, moved 1 million-plus albums worldwide, and scored a gold certification for the single “I’d Rather Be With You.” His music has appeared in over 200 films, television series, and commercials. In addition to multiple showstopping appearances on Ellen (who also enlisted him to perform at her wedding) and Today Show, and performances on The Tonight Show, Jimmy Kimmel LIVE!, and Conan, he contributed “Brand New Day” to a commercial in support of the troops at the request of First Ladies Michelle Obama and Dr. Jill Biden. He’s played to sold out crowds around the globe and shared the stage with the likes of Ed Sheeran, Sara Bareilles, Ingrid Michaelson, Sheryl Crow, Tori Amos and more. Not to mention, he’s a staunch philanthropist who supports Little Kids Rock and North Shore Animal League America (NSALA), among others. Thus far his catalog consists of nine full-length offerings highlighted by fan favorites such as We Were Here, Simple Times, Underwater, Wax Wings, and Here, Right Now. Following the release of his 2021 acclaimed album The Ghost and The Wall, Joshua left his material existence in the rearview, grabbed a backpack, packed his guitar, picked up a pen and a pad, hit the road in search of new stories to tell. Those stories comprise though the world will tell me so, volumes one & two which were released early 2023. During 2025, he turned the page on the next chapter of his career and life with his tenth full-length LP and first independent album since 2017, One Day Home. Immersing himself in the process mind, body, and soul, he pored over these 13 tracks, perfecting each moment and co-producing six tracks with Wally Gagel. This time around, he prepared the music for a double-LP release with one half original studio versions of the tracklisting and the other piano vocal versions. Musically, he taps into two sides of his sonic palette, leaning into soul and singer-songwriter stylings while tracing the journey of a romantic relationship. VIP package includes one general admission ticket and admission to an intimate pre-show event with Joshua Radin, includes: play a few songs participate in a small Q&A session Meet & Greet + Photo Op – Signed Tour Poster Crowd Free opportunity to buy merch with 10% discounted merch prices.

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: Learning that Transforms: Michigan Stories
events.summary: We all have a story about learning: an “aha!” moment, an unexpected detour, a mistake, or an experience that changed our perspective about ourselves or the world around us. Your story might come from a classroom, research lab, workplace, creative project, community, or everyday life. Maybe you tried something new, made an unexpected discovery, worked through a setback, or learned from something that didn’t go as planned. Wherever and however your learning happened, we’d love to hear about it. In this workshop, you'll develop and shape your story with Satori Shakoor, founder of Detroit’s Secret Society of Twisted Storytellers and a 2017 Kresge Literary Arts Fellow. With Satori’s guidance, you’ll discover what makes your story yours and bring it to life. Come curious and open. No storytelling experience—or polished story—is needed. After the workshop, you’ll have the option to record your story on video or share it at a live storytelling event in spring 2027. Interested? Fill out a short form to tell us about yourself: https://forms.gle/GviufLcuXTm4rPcc9 Space is limited to 10 people per workshop. The project team will begin reviewing submissions after Oct. 29 and will offer places on a rolling basis until all sessions are full. Early submissions are encouraged for the best chance of receiving a preferred date. This workshop is part of Learning That Transforms: Michigan Stories, a storytelling and video project inviting U-M students, faculty, and staff to share their personal learning stories. The project is sponsored by the Eileen Lappin Weiser Center for the Learning Sciences, and is supported by the University of Michigan's Life-Changing Education Initiative. Questions? Contact Program Manager Heidi Bennett at heidiab@umich.edu.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.
events.imageAlt: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them

events.title: The Tree of Eternity
events.summary: The Tree of Eternity is an immersive, interactive installation that explores remembrance, loss, and the enduring presence of those we have loved. The installation centers on a projected tree surrounded by interactive terminal pods that control its structure. Visitors approach interactive pods positioned throughout the gallery space, where they are invited to recall memories of people or experiences throughout their lives. Depending on the kiosk they interact with, different effects will be present on the projected tree. As more visitors’ memories are inputted, the tree’s visuals adapt and change form, demonstrating that our memories persist with us. Projection mapping creates ethereal visuals accompanied by atmospheric audio. Even when visitors aren't actively engaging with the kiosks, the system generates ambient transmissions, suggesting that the tree—and the memories it embodies—continues to live and grow. The installation creates a dialogue between life and death, presence and absence, individual memory and collective remembrance, inviting participants to contribute to a living memorial that persists beyond any single moment of grief or reflection.

events.title: Regularization by Common Noise for Mean Field Games and Mean Field Control
events.summary: A fundamental challenge in the theory of mean field games (MFGs) is that equilibria are generally non-unique in the absence of monotonicity assumptions. In this talk, we establish that an infinite-dimensional multiplicative common noise restores uniqueness for generic MFGs in one spatial dimension. Furthermore, by exploiting the connection between mean field control (MFC) and potential MFGs, we show that this common noise regularizes the MFC value function. Based on this regularity, we then construct optimal feedback controls for the MFC problem. This talk is based on joint work with F. Delarue.

events.title: FULL CIRCLE
events.summary: A circle can represent a beginning, an ending, and everything in between: movement, connection, repetition, growth, and return. FULL CIRCLE brings together artists exploring the many ways circles appear in our world and our lives. Through rings, spirals, patterns, cycles of nature, relationships, memory, transformation, and renewal, the exhibition considers what it means to come full circle.

events.title: AIA Lecture | Ariadne’s Thread: Weaving 200,000 Years of Naxos’ History
events.summary: This lecture asks, (1) what makes us (*Homo sapiens*) special? And (2) why did Theseus and Ariadne go to Naxos? These radically different questions are answered through the archaeology of Stelida, a site on the northwest coast of Naxos (Cycladic islands, Greece), whose deep-time history takes us from Neanderthal toolmakers, via Bronze Age worshippers, to the Canadian/Greek project that has been investigating the site since 2013. From the earliest seafarers of the Northern Hemisphere to Ariadne’s hill, follow this remarkable thread with the project’s director. This event is free and open to the public, sponsored by the Ann Arbor Society of the Archaeological Institute of America. Please join us in Room 125 of the Kelsey Museum’s Newberry Hall to hear from Dr. Tristan Carter, professor of anthropology at McMaster University and director of the Stelida Naxos Archaeological Project. Light refreshments will be served at 5:30 PM, followed by the lecture at 6:00 PM. If you have any questions or concerns regarding accessing this event, please visit our accessibility page at https://myumi.ch/zwPkd or contact the education office by calling (734) 647-4167. We ask for advance notice as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Mahler’s Symphony No. 6
events.summary: No warm‑ups, no safety nets. Mahler’s Sixth Symphony hits hard: from its relentless opening march, to its fragile and haunted slow movement, to the hammer-blows of fate at its close. Jader Bignamini leads the DSO through the storm, pushing players to their expressive limits. This is Mahler without filters. Visceral, searching, unforgettable. Join us for a pre-concert talk 1 hour before most performances (read more below). Enjoy this concert online at any of the following locations on Saturday, December 5 at 8:00pm ET: Live from Orchestra Hall: livefromorchestrahall.vhx.tv/live-broadcasts YouTube Live: youtube.com/@detroitsymphony/streams Facebook Live: facebook.com/detroitsymphony Pre-concert Talk Join us one hour prior to most classical performances for a 30-minute pre-concert talk. Pre-concert talks are an opportunity for conductors, musicians, and other experts to share more about the music and enhance your connection to the evening's program. You will get a glimpse into the composer's inspiration, the story behind a work, what to look for in a soloist's performance, and more! With a deeper understanding of the music, your symphony experience will be more engaging and even more memorable. Please note, our pre-concert talks are scheduled for every PVS Classical Series performance, except Friday morning Coffee Concerts. Insider tip: Seating for pre-concert talks is general admission in Orchestra Hall. Try out a different seat or section from your ticket for a new perspective.
